big: A new fund opens at ₹10 a unit and the brochure says "get in at the start". Your client sees an older fund at ₹500 and thinks ₹10 must be the bargain. It is one of the oldest myths in the market.

lines: The old fund's NAV is ₹500 and the NFO is only ₹10. Surely ₹10 is the cheaper one?
Put ₹50,000 into each, give them the same portfolio, and watch what the same market does to both.

alt: Bars comparing units bought, value after a 12 percent rise, and percentage gain for a fund at 10 rupees and a fund at 500 rupees
caps: Same ₹50,000, same stocks inside. NAV ₹10 buys 5,000 units. NAV ₹500 buys 100.
The shared portfolio rises 12%. Both unit prices rise 12%: to ₹11.20 and to ₹560.
Both holdings are now worth ₹56,000. The gain is ₹6,000 either way.
Returns are percentages. The NAV level is only where the counting started.

h: When an NFO earns a place
alt: A shield with good and weak reasons to recommend a new fund offer
caps: An NFO has no record to judge. It must earn its place on strategy, team and fit.
A real gap in the plan, plus a clear strategy and cost: good reasons.
The ₹10 price and the launch buzz say nothing about future returns.
title: Reasons to recommend an NFO
stops: Fills a real gap in the client's plan
Strategy, team and cost are clear
₹10 NAV leaves more room to grow
Launch buzz signals a coming rally

intro: Four questions, asked in this order.
rows: 1. Does an existing fund do this?
If so, compare record and cost
Name it in the client's plan
note: A new fund also starts in cash and needs time to build its portfolio, so its first months say little about the strategy.

q: A client has ₹1,00,000 for an NFO at ₹10 or an existing fund at ₹250. Both hold the same portfolio at the same cost, and it rises 8%. Which ends higher?
opts: The NFO, since 10,000 units beat 400 units
The existing fund, since its high NAV shows quality
Both end at ₹1,08,000; only the unit count differs
The NFO, but only once a full year has passed
why: More units do not mean more money. 10,000 units at ₹10.80 and 400 units at ₹270 are both ₹1,08,000.
A high NAV is only the history of past gains, not a sign of quality. The portfolio is the same, so the result is the same.
Both rise 8% on ₹1,00,000. The NAV level changes how many units you hold, never the percentage return you earn.
Time changes nothing here. The same portfolio gives the same percentage return, so a year adds no edge for the NFO.

q: A client prefers the NFO because the older fund's NAV has already run up while the NFO starts from scratch. What is the sound reply?
opts: Higher NAV is just past growth; judge on strategy and cost
He is right: a low starting NAV leaves more room to rise
He is right, but only for funds launched in a rising market
He is wrong, because older funds always beat new ones
why: NAV records past percentage gains. Room to rise depends on the portfolio and the market, so strategy and cost decide.
Room to rise belongs to the portfolio, not to the unit price. A ₹10 unit has no head start over a ₹500 one.
The market phase at launch does not change what NAV means. It still is just a starting number.
No rule says older funds win. Many records fade, and some newer funds fill gaps, so each case needs checking.

q: Which of these NFOs could you consider recommending, after the usual checks of cost and process?
opts: A flexi-cap fund much like three existing ones, launched at ₹10
A thematic fund pitched on how hot the theme is right now
A fund copying an older fund's strategy at a higher expense ratio
A new index fund covering a gap in her plan that no fund fills
why: It duplicates what exists with a long record. The ₹10 price adds nothing, and she would hold the same stocks twice.
A hot theme is a reason for caution. A late buyer is most tempted then, and a new fund has no record to test.
The same strategy at a higher cost is worse than the older twin, which at least has a track record to examine.
A real gap, named in her plan and checked on cost and process, is the case where an NFO can earn its place.

q: An AMC pitches a new mid-cap NFO by quoting the 5-year record of its older mid-cap fund, which has a different manager. What does that record tell you about the NFO?
opts: It proves the NFO will repeat that record, as both are mid-cap
Some context on the house's process; judge the NFO's own team
Nothing at all, since fund houses never share a process
It matters only if the NFO's NAV is below that fund's NAV
why: A record belongs to its manager and mandate. Same category does not mean same people, size or portfolio, so no proof follows.
The house process may carry over, but the NFO's manager, size and mandate are its own, and they are what you buy.
Houses do share research and risk rules. The record is not worthless, but it is not the NFO's own either.
NAV levels have no bearing on how much a record applies. The link depends on the team and mandate, not the unit price.

pts: A ₹10 NAV is not cheap and a ₹500 NAV is not dear. Returns are percentages, not price levels.
An NFO has no record, so judge its strategy, team, cost and fit to the client's plan.
Recommend an NFO only when it fills a real gap that existing funds do not.
